why-people-are-targeted.overview: People are targeted because attacking a person is cheaper than attacking a system, and because a person holds the authority a system will accept. Understanding this is what turns awareness from a lecture into a working instinct.
how_it_works: Social engineering works by creating a situation where the victim applies their own judgement in the attacker's favour.
It attacks the decision to trust, not the ability to detect a fake domain or read a header.
Urgency, authority, curiosity and helpfulness are the levers, and each one bypasses a different habit.
A well-researched target is far easier to attack, which is why public information is the preparation stage.
The most effective control is a procedure, because a procedure interrupts the moment of decision in a way awareness alone does not.
history: Early confidence tricks needed only a plausible story, because systems relied almost entirely on physical trust.
The internet removed the need for in-person contact, which made targeting scalable and anonymous.
Social networks turned personal information into a searchable database, which improved targeting quality dramatically.
Organisations moved from awareness campaigns to a behaviour change model, since attendance numbers proved nothing.
real_world: An attacker who knows a target's project, manager and holiday dates can build a message that needs no deception at all.
The same request sent to a hundred people in a company usually finds one person with the right combination of access and trust.
Reporting rises immediately after a public incident and then fades, which is exactly when the next wave arrives.
what_to_look_for: Check how decisions are made: if one person's judgement is the only control, that person is the target.
Check how much about your organisation is publicly inferable, and whether any of it aids a targeted approach.
Check whether there is a defined process for unusual requests, or whether people improvise.
Check whether people can report something without admitting they were fooled, which determines whether you ever hear about it.
defensive: Put a procedure in front of the decision, so verification happens before action rather than after.
Make out-of-band verification the default for anything touching money, credentials or access.
Reduce the public detail available about who does what, since it is preparation for someone else.
Train on recognition of pressure and urgency rather than on lists of suspicious words.
Make reporting cheap and blameless, because the incidents you never hear about are the ones you cannot measure.

phishing-anatomy-of-a-message.overview: A phishing message is a request delivered by a channel you already trust. Learning to read one properly is more useful than learning to spot a bad link, because the link is the part that changes.
how_it_works: The message establishes a plausible context first, so the request feels like a continuation of something already in progress.
A call to action is the point of the message, and everything else exists to make the action seem ordinary.
The sender identity is the easiest thing to fake, and the display name in particular proves nothing.
A link's visible text and its real destination are independent, which is why hovering and reading is a real check.
A message that creates urgency or fear reduces the reader's willingness to verify, which is the whole objective.
history: Bulk phishing produced a huge volume of obviously bad messages, which trained people to be sceptical at a low threshold.
Spear phishing reduced volume and improved personalisation, which reset that threshold in attackers' favour.
Business email compromise refined the approach further by removing any technical trick at all.
Email authentication standards reduced spoofing of the domain, which pushed attackers toward impersonating a real colleague instead.
real_world: A message from a real colleague's compromised account is technically perfect, so header and domain checks find nothing.
A password reset prompt that leads to a lookalike domain defeats a user who only checks that the page looks right.
An attachment in a thread the user started, replying to something they actually sent, defeats careful inspection of the thread.
what_to_look_for: Check the actual sender address and reply-to, not the display name.
Check where the link goes before clicking, and prefer navigating to a known address instead.
Check whether the request is urgent, unusual, or bypasses a process you normally follow.
Check whether the message expects you to reveal a credential, a code, or payment details.
defensive: Teach people to hover and read the destination, and to type known addresses rather than follow links.
Require multi-factor authentication so a successful phishing attempt does not mean account access.
Use a separate mailbox for external mail and payment requests, so the ordinary inbox is not the place where trust is tested.
Add a banner marking external or unverified senders, and expect people to read it.
Make reporting a single click, and monitor the report rate as a real security metric.

vishing-smishing-and-quishing.overview: The same social engineering works over voice, text and QR codes. Each channel has its own weaknesses, and each exploits something different about how people behave in that medium.
how_it_works: Voice works because it creates real time pressure and because the caller can react to what the target says.
A caller who already knows internal terminology, a name or a project detail has credibility immediately.
Text is limited in length, which pushes attackers to use brevity and a single clear instruction.
A QR code moves the target to a physical-looking action, which bypasses the habit of reading a URL before visiting it.
The common thread is a request to change channel, break process, or act before verifying.
history: Cold-calling support desks was an early and effective technique, and largely stopped once verification improved.
Voice phishing returned with the availability of caller identity spoofing and cheap international calling.
Text messaging gained traction once business communication moved to phones.
QR codes created a new delivery channel precisely because scanning does not involve reading an address.
real_world: A caller claiming to be from the service desk, already knowing the employee name, is routinely convincing.
A message about a failed delivery is expected, so a link in it is not surprising.
A code of conduct or parking notice placed in a car park is a genuine lure rather than a mistake.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the caller already knows things they should not, and treat internal knowledge as suspicious rather than reassuring.
Check whether the request moves to another channel, which is the point where the original trust stops applying.
Check whether you are being asked to bypass a process, especially for a supposedly urgent account issue.
Check whether the message arrives on a channel you did not expect to hear from that person on.
defensive: Publish one verified number for the service desk, and instruct staff to call back on it rather than accept an incoming call.
Never ask for a one-time code, password or remote access in response to an unsolicited contact.
Verify payment or credential changes through a channel the requester did not initiate.
Treat an unexpected code of conduct or payment request as a reportable event, not a minor irritation.
Practise the call-back habit explicitly, because it is the control that works across every channel.

pretexting-baiting-and-tailgating.overview: Not every social engineering attack involves a message. Some involve a person walking in, being helpful, or simply following the crowd through a door they should not have opened.
how_it_works: A pretext is a story that explains why the person is asking, and it works when the story fits the situation.
Physical pretexts work in a specific place, so a delivery uniform in a loading bay is more effective than in a café.
Baiting leaves something appealing in a place the target will go, turning the target's own behaviour into the delivery.
Tailgating needs no deception at all; it relies on someone holding a door and not wanting to make a scene.
All three succeed because the socially correct action and the secure action are different, and the secure one is awkward.
history: Physical access was the original boundary, and it was guarded by a person at a desk.
Access control badges and mantraps replaced the person, which raised the bar for entry.
Organisations moved to self-service and contactless entry, which removed the human checkpoint entirely.
Physical attacks returned as a targeting mechanism once technical entry was hardened, especially against high-value premises.
real_world: An unverified contractor walking through a secure area is a routine and largely unreported event.
A USB drive left in a car park is a low-technology, low-cost and still effective route into an organisation.
Someone carrying an awkward load through a door is accepted without anyone deciding to accept them.
what_to_look_for: Check what your reception process actually does when someone has no appointment, no badge, or no host.
Check whether delivery and contractor entry is separated from general visitor entry.
Check whether anyone challenges an unknown person without needing permission from a manager first.
Check whether there is a defined procedure for a suspicious item found on the premises.
defensive: Make badge-only access the rule, and train staff to challenge rather than to accommodate.
Require escorts for anyone without a business reason to be in the area, including maintenance.
Issue a short, specific procedure for visitors with no appointment, so the decision is not improvised.
Train staff that holding a door is not a security decision they are expected to make alone.
Report anything left or found, since a baited device is only a threat once someone picks it up.

business-email-compromise-and-payment-fr.overview: Business email compromise is the most financially damaging form of social engineering because it involves no malware and no technical flaw. It is a convincing message plus a changed bank detail.
how_it_works: The usual pattern is a thread with a real conversation in it, ending with a request to pay a different account.
The attacker may have read the thread through a compromised mailbox, which is why the context is accurate.
A change of bank details should be the trigger for verification, and the request arrives at exactly the moment that step is easiest to skip.
Payment processes that allow a single person to change details and release payment give the attack somewhere to land.
The loss is often recoverable, but only if it is reported within a short window.
history: Advance fee fraud is the long-running predecessor, and it is still running.
Email account compromise removed the need for any technical skill, since anyone can read a mailbox.
Organisations responded with callback verification procedures, which attackers then learned to work around.
The current model combines mailbox access, a real conversation and a payment process with a single point of control.
real_world: A supplier's real mailbox is compromised, and a genuine-looking invoice arrives with new bank details for the first time.
The change is requested during a period of high volume, when verification feels like an obstacle.
An urgent CEO request for a confidential purchase bypasses the normal purchase approval route.
what_to_look_for: Check whether any bank detail change is verified by a known phone number rather than by replying to the message.
Check whether payment release and supplier-detail change can be done by the same person.
Check whether executives can request payments that bypass the normal route, and whether anyone verifies them.
Check how quickly a fraudulent payment can be reported and recalled.
defensive: Verify every change of payment details out of band, using a number you already had, not one in the message.
Separate the ability to change supplier details from the ability to release a payment.
Add a defined route for executive payment requests, with a verification step that is always required.
Limit the number of people who can approve payments, and require two for anything unusual.
Rehearse the recall process, because speed is the only thing that recovers the money.

insider-threat-motive-opportunity-detect.overview: The phrase insider threat covers several different situations, and lumping them together leads to bad controls. Malicious insiders and negligent insiders need entirely different responses.
how_it_works: Motive, opportunity and capability are the three factors, and opportunity is the one an organisation controls directly.
Most insider incidents are accidental or negligent rather than malicious, and that changes the whole response.
A departing employee with abrupt behaviour, or one with a grievance, is a recognised risk signal.
Over-broad access makes every mistake and every malicious act far more damaging.
Detection usually comes from a behaviour change relative to a baseline, not from a single action.
history: Early monitoring was limited to what an employee did with a file, which missed data sent to personal accounts.
Data loss prevention tools expanded visibility to email, removable media and cloud uploads.
Analytic platforms made it possible to baseline normal behaviour and alert on deviation.
Legal and privacy constraints in several jurisdictions limit how far behavioural monitoring can go, which is a genuine constraint.
real_world: An employee copying a customer database to a personal drive before resigning is one of the most common insider data events.
A well-meaning administrator bulk-exporting data for a migration creates the same exposure with no intent at all.
A shared account means an insider action cannot be attributed, which blocks the investigation entirely.
what_to_look_for: Check who can reach sensitive data, and whether that matches their current role rather than their history.
Check whether access is removed promptly and automatically when a person changes role or leaves.
Check whether bulk data movement is visible and alerted on.
Check whether actions can be attributed to a person, since shared accounts defeat this.
defensive: Apply least privilege continuously, so no single person can take data they have no business touching.
Remove access automatically on the leaver trigger, and make exceptions visible.
Use unique individual accounts everywhere, including for administrators.
Alert on bulk export and on access to data the person does not normally need.
Handle the negligent case with better tooling and clearer rules, since that is where the majority of incidents are.

reporting-culture-and-channels.overview: You cannot defend against what nobody tells you about. A reporting rate that is implausibly low is a signal about the culture, not about the absence of incidents.
how_it_works: Every report is free information, and every suppressed report is an incident you will learn about later and more expensively.
People hide mistakes when the response to a mistake is worse than the response to an incident.
The reporting channel has to be easier than the alternative of saying nothing.
Reports need to be acted on visibly, or the channel dies.
Time to report is itself a security metric, because it drives how many victims there are.
history: Reporting was rare and often treated as an admission of failure, which suppressed exactly the information defenders needed.
Awareness programmes began to include reporting as an explicit objective rather than a secondary benefit.
Phishing report buttons made reporting a single action, which raised volumes sharply.
Organisations matured to treating reported events as the normal input to detection engineering rather than as a problem.
real_world: A user who clicked a link and did not report it means an entire campaign succeeds because of one non-report.
A team with a low report rate usually has low trust, and often has more incidents than a team with a high one.
A reported suspicious email is often a compromise of somebody else's account, so one report protects many people.
what_to_look_for: Check how many people used the reporting channel last month, and whether that number moves at all.
Check what happens to a person after a report, and whether anyone has asked.
Check whether there is a channel that does not require opening a ticket or talking to a manager.
Check whether reports are fed back to the people who made them.
defensive: Make reporting one action, available from email and from the tool bar, with no justification required.
Respond to reports with a visible outcome, even when the outcome is that it was harmless.
Train explicitly that reporting a mistake early is the behaviour being wanted.
Measure report volume, time to report and report quality, and treat a drop as a warning.
Give the security team the authority to act on a report without a management approval step.

security-awareness-that-changes-behaviou.overview: Most awareness programmes measure attendance and satisfaction, neither of which predicts behaviour. The programmes that work change what people do at the moment of decision, and they are usually cheaper than the ones that do not.
how_it_works: Training is most effective immediately before the moment it is needed, and least effective as an annual module.
Feedback that is immediate and personal teaches more than a score, because it connects the action to the outcome.
Simulated exercises work when they are used to measure and improve, and backfire when people are punished for them.
A control that removes the need for a decision beats training for that decision.
Metrics should be behavioural: report rates, verification rates, and how many bad actions were caught by a process rather than by luck.
history: Annual compliance training was the default for years and was widely regarded as ineffective.
Behaviour-based frameworks reframed the objective from remembering rules to performing actions.
Phishing simulations became standard, and were initially used punitively before being corrected.
Current practice pushes the decision upstream: build the process so the error is harder to commit in the first place.
real_world: A team trained annually still falls for the same message, because the training was six months ago.
A callback procedure reduces successful payment fraud more than any awareness course did.
A simulation used to punish people produces under-reporting, which removes the visibility you were trying to create.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the programme measures behaviour or only completion.
Check whether the exercises result in a concrete change, such as a new process or a changed control.
Check whether people are told what to do, not only what not to do.
Check whether the material is specific to the ways your own organisation is actually attacked.
defensive: Prefer a control that removes the decision entirely, and fall back to training only for what remains.
Refresh material on a real incident in your organisation while it is still relevant.
Measure verification and reporting rates, and compare against a baseline rather than against other companies.
Use simulations to improve systems, and never to shame individuals.
Give people a specific script for the two or three situations they are most likely to face.

personal-social-footprint-and-osint.overview: Everything an attacker wants to know about you is already public, and the aggregation is worse than any individual post. Reviewing that footprint is the most directly useful thing a person can do for their own security.
how_it_works: Public profiles combine employment, location, relationships and interests into a targeting package.
People search for your data before they contact you, so the search results are part of your security boundary.
A data broker sells the same aggregation to anyone who asks, and organisations often cannot remove it.
Metadata in published photos and documents can disclose location, device and account names.
A strong, reused password tied to an identifiable email address turns a small breach into a targeted one.
history: Personal information was collected mainly by employers, credit agencies and the state.
Social networks made self-disclosure voluntary and constant, and made it searchable.
Data brokers emerged to assemble profiles from those sources, including some that people never knowingly published.
Search engines and people-search services made the assembled profile trivially accessible to anyone.
real_world: A phishing message that references a real conference talk and a real colleague is far more effective than a generic one.
A reused password from a decade-old breach site, applied to an email address with a known employer, is enough for a targeted attack.
Photos of a home office, a badge or a whiteboard disclose more than their owner intended.
what_to_look_for: Search your own name, your email address and your username, and read what is actually indexed.
Check which accounts you have, including ones you stopped using years ago.
Check whether the same password is used anywhere you still care about.
Check what your public posts reveal about location, working hours and relationships.
defensive: Use a different, generated password for every account, with a manager to keep track of them.
Enable multi-factor authentication on the accounts that can reach your email, since email resets everything else.
Review privacy settings on social platforms, and assume anything posted publicly is permanent.
Remove geotags from photographs and check documents for metadata before sharing.
Request removal from data brokers, accepting that coverage is partial and recheck periodically.
